Injection 6 already reached the maximum CRF, so shorten its gradient by one grid step while preserving its favorable temperature and starting composition. This tests whether the run can be accelerated while keeping the critical pair at R ≥ 1.5.

Shortening the gradient improved the minimum resolution from 1.62 to 1.67 while reducing the last retention time. Test a further reduction to 16 minutes, keeping composition and temperature fixed, to seek a faster separation that retains CRF 1.000.

Continue shortening the gradient at fixed composition and temperature: the critical pair has improved with increasing slope, and all pairs retain resolution margin. A 12-minute gradient tests a faster separation while monitoring the declining resolutions of pairs (4,5) and (6,7).

Test a faster gradient while holding composition and temperature fixed; the 12-minute method still has all resolutions above 1.97. The declining resolutions of pairs (4,5) and (6,7) will determine whether this further acceleration preserves CRF 1.000.

Shorten the gradient by one grid step to locate the fastest fully resolved method at this composition and temperature. Pairs (4,5) and (6,7) are approaching the resolution threshold, so this tests the limit while retaining injection 12 as a proven CRF 1.000 method.

Lowering phi1 to 0.65 gives a slope between the fully resolved 8-minute method and the marginal 6-minute method. This should recover resolution for the critical pair while keeping the last peak earlier than injection 12.

Raise temperature by one grid step from the fastest fully resolved method to test whether retention can be shortened without losing CRF 1.000. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates temperature selectivity effects on the two pairs near the resolution threshold.

Return to 25 C and shift the gradient window upward by 0.05 while preserving injection 14's slope. This tests whether a stronger starting composition can shorten the separation while maintaining the critical-pair resolution, without the adverse temperature shift seen in injection 15.

Halve the gradient slope relative to injection 16 while retaining its stronger starting composition and favorable temperature. This tests whether a shallower gradient restores the critical pair's resolution sufficiently to make the higher-starting-organic approach useful.

Test a lower starting organic fraction to improve the selectivity lost at phi0 0.40, using a steeper gradient to offset the added retention. At 30 C, the later close pair gained resolution in injection 15, which may help it tolerate this faster gradient.

Lower only the temperature from injection 18 to test whether the favorable 25 C selectivity restores its unresolved pair. Monitor the later close pair, since cooling may reduce its resolution; injection 14 remains the fastest proven CRF 1.000 method.

At 30 C the later close pair was well resolved, but the middle pair needs a shallower gradient. Reduce the slope from 0.075 to 0.050 organic fraction per minute to test whether both pairs can reach R ≥ 1.5 in a compact gradient window.

Use a moderately shallower slope than injection 19 to improve both marginal pairs while retaining the favorable 25 C selectivity. This tests whether a four-minute programmed gradient can achieve full resolution, with injection 14 retained as the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Revisit 30 C with a shallower gradient than injection 15 to recover its unresolved middle pair while preserving the improved late-pair separation. The 0.35 starting fraction also provided more middle-pair resolution than 0.30 in the tested gradients.

Trim injection 14's gradient to four minutes while preserving its starting composition, temperature, and slope. The outlet gradient ends at 4.65 minutes, after its observed last peak at 4.14 minutes, so this should preserve CRF 1.000 with a shorter programmed gradient.

The maximum CRF is already secured, so test a slightly shallower gradient near the fastest successful method to increase its resolution margin. This should improve both limiting pairs while keeping the last peak comfortably below the 10-minute penalty threshold.

Use the final injection to test a compact four-minute gradient with a slightly shallower slope than injection 24, seeking additional resolution margin while remaining well below the time-penalty threshold. Injection 23 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.
